newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - September 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - September 16.

text.p: -- BANK CHIEF HAILS EMU PROSPECTS

In an interview with the Financial Times newspaper, Bank of England governor Eddie George claimed that the City of London stands to reap large benefits from European monetary union (Emu), even if it is not among the founder members. But George qualified his enthusiasm by emphasising that member countries must not act in their own narrow national interest, and warned that the dispute between Britain, France and Germany over access to a future EU interbank payment system needs to be resolved.
-- TOP COMMERCIAL LAW FIRMS SEE RETURN OF 1980S BOOM

The top commercial law firms in the UK are reporting levels of income comparable to those in the 'boom' of the late 1980's. The top 100 firms billed 3.25 billion stg in fees in 1995-96, up 250 million stg from the previous year and 500 million more than in 1992-93. A survey to be published Monday also reveals that senior partners at the City's top-paying firm, Slaughter & May, earned 560,000 stg last year.
-- COMPULSORY INSURANCE URGED FOR CARE OF ELDERLY

Social research charity the Joseph Rowntree Foundation is to publish an independent report into the funding of long-term care for the elderly which recommends that the UK should introduce compulsory national insurance. Funds raised by the national care insurance scheme would be managed by the private sector - a suggestion which goes even further than the government's own proposals to encourage wider use of private insurance to cover long-term health costs.
-- TREASURY BENEFITED BY BILLIONS FROM STATE SELL-OFFS

A report commissioned by the Conservative think-tank the Centre for Policy Studies and due to be published Monday will reveal that the Treasury has benefited by up to 11.5 billion stg a year for the past ten years due to the privatisation of state companies. The report looked at 33 British companies sold off since the early 1980s - including British Telecom and British Steel - and is likely to add further fuel to Labour claims that many companies were sold off too cheaply.
-- RAIL CHAOS THREAT EASES AFTER DEAL

Two more regional rail operating companies have been spared planned industrial action after reaching agreement with the RMT union over working hours and some performance bonus payments. The settlements mean that ten of the 24 operating companies have struck deals with unions. However, nine of the other operators still face strike action next Monday, with seven of these also facing action this Friday.
-- CHANNEL 5 AWARDED EXTRA FREQUENCIES

The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is expected to announce Monday approval for Channel 5 to use extra frequencies, increasing the coverage of the new broadcaster from 70 per cent to 78 per cent. The new capacity has been taken from channel 35, which has so far been reserved for mobile digital terrestrial television. But Channel 5 will have use of the frequency for a minimum of five years, as no-one has yet expressed an interest in mobile digital television.
-- TELECOMS GROUPS ABILITY DOUBTED ON MULTIMEDIA

A long-term research study sponsored by the DTI and a number of interested companies has made an interim conclusion that the UK's telecommunications operators are poorly organised to benefit from their customer' ambitions to move into 'electronic commerce', and that competitors such as Electronic Data Systems or Sema Group will take advantage. The study is highly critical of the capabilities of all the licensed telecoms operators in the UK, including BT and Mercury.
-- SOFTWARE RIVALS FACE ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST SALVO

An industry forum in Paris is anticipating the so-called 'battle of the billionaires' as both Bill Gates of Microsoft and Larry Ellison of Oracle are scheduled to speak. The event comes 12 months after Ellison sparked a bitter battle with Gates by claiming the Personal Computer was doomed and would be replaced by his own 'network computer'. Both men are expected to present their versions of the future for home computing.
-- BAe WILL NOT LIFT AIRBUS STAKE

British Aerospace is not to increase its 20 per cent stake in Airbus Industrie after accepting that such a move would be politically unacceptable in Germany and France. The UK company will instead look for other ways to safeguard its interests in Airbus. The BAe decision comes as Airbus prepares for the lengthy process of becoming a limited company.
-- HEAD OF SONY'S STRUGGLING FILM DIVISION OUSTED

Sony's troubled film division has been thrown into fresh crisis after the ousting of its top executive and the subsequent refusal of the job by the man expected to replace him. The debacle throws into doubt the future of other top executives, both in Los Angeles and at the group's New York headquarters. Sony has been struggling in the firm industry for six years now, and the latest crisis may even prompt the group to seek a partner in the entertainment industry.
